cards.title: Amazon Individual vs Professional Selling Plan Decision
cards.summary: Choosing between Amazon's Individual ($0.99/unit) and Professional ($39.99/mo) plan determines Buy Box eligibility, ungating capability, and monthly cost structure.
cards.use_when: Deciding which Amazon selling plan to register for when opening a seller account, based on expected monthly volume and whether you need Buy Box or brand ungating.
steps: Compare cost structures: the source states the Individual plan charges per-unit fees (she cites ~$1/unit) plus other selling fees and caps you at under 40 units/month, while the Professional plan is a flat monthly fee (she cites $39.99/mo) with unlimited units.
Note the strategic constraint: per the source, Individual sellers cannot win the Buy Box (the featured offer that drives most sales) and face much harder brand/category ungating and restrictions.

If you expect steady volume and need ungating or Buy Box access, the source recommends starting on Professional; if you are genuinely unsure whether you'll commit, start Individual to avoid recurring fees.
Both plans require the first month's Professional fee (~$39.99) at signup per the source — confirm current pricing and rules on Seller Central before deciding, as fees change.

Prepare at signup: government-issued ID (passport or driver's license), a debit or credit card, bank routing/account number, tax info (SSN or EIN), phone, and email (source suggests a separate business email).
caveats: Fees and plan rules cited are from a January 2025 video and change frequently — verify current Seller Central terms.
The source is a reseller/arbitrage seller; plan choice guidance is framed around that model.

cards.title: Brand and Category Ungating Process for Resellers
cards.summary: Amazon requires approval (ungating) per brand and category before you can list established-brand products, and denials are common so you must reapply repeatedly with invoices and photos.
cards.use_when: When you want to list a branded product on Amazon and are blocked by a gating restriction, or planning which categories/brands to pursue for reselling.
steps: Identify which brands/categories are gated by checking the listing in your sourcing tool (e.g., SellerAmp shows if you're ungated or need approval).

Purchase the required units from a wholesaler, distributor, or authorized reseller to generate an invoice — the source cites 10 units historically but notes Amazon has sometimes required 100; try your existing 10-unit invoices first.
Submit the invoice plus, often, photos of the total units you purchased.
Expect denials and reapply: the source reports being approved for grocery on her 4th application, and hearing of approvals on the 10th or 20th attempt.
Make key details stand out on your application (highlighting what reviewers need to see), since the source notes reviewers process applications quickly and highlights can speed approval.
Aim to get ungated across roughly 10–15 brands/categories before scaling sourcing and software spend.
To avoid gating entirely on your own product line, note the source's contrast: private label (your own brand, not reselling established products) does not require this reseller ungating process.
caveats: Unit thresholds and approval odds are the source's anecdotal experience, not Amazon policy — requirements vary by category and change.
Ungating applies to reselling established brands, not private label.

cards.title: Reseller Software Stack: SellerAmp, Keepa, SellerBoard
cards.summary: Three tools cover sourcing analysis, price/trend history, and reimbursement-plus-review automation for an Amazon reselling business, each with a different trigger point for adoption.
cards.use_when: Deciding which Amazon seller tools to buy and when, to avoid paying for software before you have listings or are already selling.
steps: Use SellerAmp for product sourcing analysis: monthly sales volume, competition/seller count, their stock and prices, whether you're ungated, IP/private-label alerts, and Buy Box win percentages per seller.
Use Keepa for price history and trend tracking on a product over time — critical for judging whether a current price is stable or likely to drop.

Delay software purchases until after you've gotten ungated for brands/categories, because these tools bill monthly and there's no analytical value before you can actually source approved products, per the source.

Add SellerBoard only once you have active listings — it tracks whether Amazon received all your units, provides a template for reimbursement claims for lost units, automates review-request emails (source says ~5 days after delivery), and tracks Amazon fees.
See if free trials or extended trials (source cites a 2-month SellerBoard trial) are available before committing to paid annual/monthly plans.
Watch tutorials to learn each tool's workflow before relying on it for live sourcing decisions.
caveats: Tool capabilities, pricing, and trials change — verify current features and terms.
The source derives income/affiliate links from some tools, so treat recommendations with that in mind.

cards.title: Sourcing Method Choice: Retail vs Online Arbitrage
cards.summary: Retail arbitrage offers less competition and better in-store deals but isn't scalable, while online arbitrage is scalable at the cost of faster competition and price decay.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to source inventory for a reselling operation, or diagnosing why sourced products arrive already devalued and saturated.
steps: Choose retail arbitrage (in-store scanning with SellerAmp) if you're a beginner wanting less listing competition and occasional better deals — but accept it is not scalable since you must physically buy, carry, prep, and ship each unit.
Choose online arbitrage (sourcing from online retailers shipped to you or a prep center) when you want to scale, since you can source from a computer without store visits.

Account for online arbitrage's downside: the source notes the same profitable product can be found by others quickly, so a product whose price is high when found may drop by $10–$20 by the time it arrives, leaving you unprofitable.
Do genuine due diligence per product (volume, seller count, price history) rather than relying on a quick find — the source attributes common losses to lazy, shallow sourcing.
Trial both methods to see which fits your time and capital, then shift toward online sourcing as you scale.
caveats: Retail/online arbitrage economics and failure modes differ from private label — the source explicitly notes this is reselling established brands, not own-brand DTC.
Price-decay and saturation risks are the source's general observations, not fixed benchmarks.

cards.title: Reading FBA Inventory Breakdown: FC Transfer, FC Processing, Reserved
cards.summary: Use Seller Central's FBA inventory breakdown to diagnose where units are between shipment and sellable, and interpret FC transfer vs FC processing vs reserved states.
cards.use_when: When units you shipped to Amazon are not yet sellable and you need to know where they are, whether they're lost, or when to escalate for reimbursement.
steps: Go to Seller Central → Manage All Inventory, and under the SKU condition scroll to the FBA Inventory Breakdown section.

Read the statuses: 'FC transfer' means Amazon is dispersing units among different fulfillment centers; 'FC processing' means units are at their final warehouse being opened, scanned in, and shelved — this phase takes a while.
Expect transit to Amazon to be fast (source cites ~3–4 days) but check-in/processing to be the long part.
Benchmark timing: the source considers 1–2 weeks for check-in normal; beyond 2 weeks she begins investigating reimbursement, though Q4 (Oct–Dec) check-in can legitimately take a month due to demand.
If units are not received in full, use the reimbursement process (SellerBoard provides a template to paste into Seller Support) to recover lost units.
Confirm Amazon sometimes splits one shipment across multiple fulfillment centers — seeing units in FC transfer is expected, not an error.
caveats: Timing figures are the source's experience and vary — Seller Central layout and terminology change, so verify the current interface.
Q4 delays are seasonally normal, not necessarily a lost-inventory situation.

cards.title: Prepping and Labeling Units for FBA Shipments
cards.summary: Remove original price tags and apply FNSKU labels over the UPC before shipping, so customers don't see your acquisition price and Amazon can scan your units.
cards.use_when: When prepping sourced inventory for an FBA shipment, especially clearance or discounted items that still carry store price stickers.
steps: Remove any visible price tags from the product — the source warns that a customer seeing a $5 clearance label on a $20 listing is likely to return it.
Print free 2×1 FNSKU labels from Amazon Seller Central and apply them to cover the product's UPC code.

Use standard materials: a printer, 2×1 labels, poly bags, and a label set for prepping; get 4×6 shipping labels and boxes free from carriers like UPS or by reusing boxes from local retail stores (asking which days they receive trucks).
Create the shipment in Seller Central and send units to Amazon following the current shipping workflow.
If using an outsourced prep center instead, they handle this step — the source later moved prepping to a Florida prep center and sought one in a tax-free state to avoid sales tax in the landed cost.
Do the steps yourself first before outsourcing, so you understand each part of the business.
caveats: Seller Central's shipping layout updates frequently — the workflow may look different from older tutorials.
Prep-center tax treatment depends on state; verify current tax rules and provider location.

cards.title: Repricing Listings to Stay Competitive as the Market Moves
cards.summary: Ship-and-forget listings become unprofitable as prices shift, so reprice manually at first and move to repricing software past roughly 25 active listings.
cards.use_when: After units become active on Amazon, to keep prices competitive and protect margin against price drops, or when managing a growing listing count becomes too slow to check by hand.
steps: Check newly active listings daily, since the market fluctuates and a product may drop (source example: from $50 to $30) before your units even check in.
Reprice manually in the early stage — no repricing software is needed when you have few listings.
Once you exceed roughly 25 active products, manual daily repricing becomes impractical; the source recommends investing in repricing software (she personally uses BQ).
Note that repricing software is relatively expensive compared to earlier tools, so it is justified only once listing count makes manual work unmanageable.
caveats: The ~25-listing threshold is the source's own rule of thumb, not a measured benchmark.
Repricing tool names and pricing change — verify current options and costs.

cards.title: When and How to Outsource Sourcing and Prep
cards.summary: Outsource only after you master the business yourself, starting with sourcing via trained VAs and prep via a tax-free-state prep center.
cards.use_when: When an Amazon reselling operation is stable and you want to reduce time spent on the two most time-consuming tasks — sourcing and prepping — to scale.
steps: First learn every aspect of the business yourself; the source advises beginners not to outsource anything at the start.

Outsource sourcing to trained virtual assistants — the source uses a trained-VA program and pays ~$3–4/hour (Philippines-based rate) for 40 hrs/week; she cites spending over $3,000 in one month on products that VA surfaced.
Outsource prepping to a prep center, and specifically seek one located in a tax-free state so sales tax isn't added to your cost when your VA sources product.
Recognize that prepping 'doesn't make the money' directly and is the natural second thing to offload after sourcing.
Keep sourcing and prepping as the two outsourced functions while you focus on higher-leverage work.
caveats: Wage rates and the $3,000/month sourcing spend are the source's own figures, not typical benchmarks.
Trained-VA programs and affiliate promotions can bias such recommendations — verify VA training quality independently.

cards.title: Creating the Amazon Seller Account: Required Documents and Setup
cards.summary: Assemble the required identity, payment, banking, and tax documents before signing up, and anticipate card-linking friction at registration.
cards.use_when: When registering an Amazon seller account and gathering the documents and payment methods needed to complete signup.
steps: Gather a government-issued ID (driver's license or passport — the source anecdotally heard passports may be accepted faster, unverified); no student or library cards.

Have a payment method ready for the first month's ~$39.99 fee; a debit card works even if the site implies credit-only, and if your bank isn't listed, scroll to 'other' and try different cards if linking fails.
Provide a bank routing and account number for payouts, plus tax information (SSN, or EIN if using an LLC).
Note the source's LLC timing: she formed an LLC after surpassing $10K in monthly sales (her fifth month selling), citing that an LLC is not required but is good to have.
Use a separate business email rather than a personal one (optional but recommended by the source).
Confirm you are 18+ and enter basic details (name, phone, email).
caveats: Signup fees, document rules, and UI change — verify current Seller Central requirements.
An LLC/EIN is optional for individuals; tax treatment depends on your situation.

cards.title: Sequencing the Amazon Reseller Startup: Research to First Sales
cards.summary: A beginner reseller sequence — research, open account, buy supplies, get ungated, add software, source, prep and ship, track inventory, reprice — avoids paying for tools before they're useful.
cards.use_when: When planning the order of operations for launching an Amazon reselling business and deciding what to do (and spend on) at each stage.
steps: Research the model through free content before committing capital, to confirm you want to stick with it.
Open the seller account (choose plan per volume and Buy Box needs).
Buy materials upfront (printer, 2×1 labels, poly bags) unless using a prep center.
Get ungated for the brands/categories you intend to sell — this gates your ability to source.
Only after getting ungated, buy analytical software (SellerAmp, Keepa), since tools bill monthly and are useless before you can source approved products.
Begin sourcing — the source calls this the core of the business and stresses diligence over speed.
Prep, label, and ship units; then track inventory receipt (add SellerBoard for reimbursement and review automation once listings are live).
Reprice listings as the market moves, and only later outsource sourcing and prep.
caveats: This is one reseller's workflow from a January 2025 video; tool pricing, ungating rules, and Seller Central UI have since changed.
The model shown is retail/online arbitrage reselling of established brands, not private label.
